title: How then can they require regenerating grace for every good work and condemn Trent?
source_text: XXXII. Si ergo bona opera nonnulla, ex ipsa Protestantium Doctrina & confessione, antecedunt hominis regenerationem & justificationem, quomodo statuere possunt gratiam ipsam qua regeneramur atque justificamur necessariam esse ad quodvis opus bonum, & damnare canonem Concilii Tridentini, quo anathema pronunciatur in eos qui dicunt opera omnia quae ante justificationem fiunt, quacunque ratione facta sint, vere esse peccata?
pass_a_gloss: XXXII. If therefore some good works, from the very Protestants' Doctrine and confession, precede man's regeneration and justification, how can they lay down that the very grace by which we are regenerated and justified is necessary for any good work, and condemn the canon of the Council of Trent, by which anathema is pronounced against those who say that all works which are done before justification, in whatever manner they be done, are truly sins?
pass_b_english: Thesis XXXII. So if, by the Protestants' own doctrine and admission, some good works precede a man's regeneration and justification, how can they hold that the very grace by which we are regenerated and justified is necessary for every good work?
And how can they condemn the canon of the Council of Trent that pronounces anathema on those who say that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are truly sins?

choices.why: The grace by which a man is born again and justified; the Protestants are said to require it, not merely a helping grace, for any truly good work.
